name: Marcus Beardsley

name: Eric Blum
extracted_department: Eric Blum joined the Cornell Classics department in Fall 2022. He earned his B.A. in Classical Studies summa cum laude with a minor in Linguistics from Brandeis University that same year. He is interested in Greek poetry from Homer through the fifth century, particularly the lyric of Pindar and the choral odes of tragedy. Particular focuses include pragmatic and lexicographic approaches to poetry. He is most enthralled by language which seems to actively resist being understood. His dissertation, provisionally entitled “Pindar Beyond Praise: Defeat Amid Victory in Pindar’s Ajax Poems,” argues that a priori assumptions about genre can obscure the expansive poikilia of Pindar’s poetry. The Judgment of Arms myth in particular is a story not about celebrating victory, but about acknowledging defeat even in happy circumstances.

name: Kate Hall

name: Clara McCafferty Wright
extracted_department: Clara McCafferty Wright is a doctoral student at Cornell University in Classical Archaeology and Art. Her primary research foci include Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt, and Greco-Roman reception of Egypt. She recently completed an MPhil degree in Egyptology at the University of Cambridge with a dissertation entitled, “Reconsidering Cleopatra VII: The Lost Narrative of Egypt’s Last Queen.” Clara earned her A.B. at Bryn Mawr College in 2019, where she double majored in Classical and Near Eastern Archaeology & Classical Cultures and Societies. At Bryn Mawr, she was a Hanna Holborn Gray Research Fellow and authored a thesis on Cleopatra VII’s political influence on the Isis cult in Italy. During her undergraduate degree, she also studied in the Egyptology programs at the University of Pennsylvania and the American University in Cairo. In addition, she established The Bryn Mawr College Magic Lantern Slide Digitization Project. Clara currently serves as a Director of The American Research Center in Egypt—Missouri Chapter, and a team member of the Egyptology State of the Field Survey Project. Clara is passionate about diversifying our understanding of the ancient world to one which includes the narratives of disenfranchised members of societies, including women, enslaved people, and the working class. She has a strong interest in using the study of the past to empower people today by making information on the ancient world accessible to rural and underprivileged communities.

name: Sara Merker
extracted_department: Sara is a sixth-year PhD candidate in Classical Literature and Philology whose research focuses on Greek and Latin literature of the Roman imperial period, particularly rhetoric, humor, and the performance of cultural authority. She received her BA with First Class Honours in Classics from McGill University in 2020. Her dissertation, “Humor and Religious Polemic in the Second and Third Centuries CE,” argues that authors on both sides of the modern divide between ‘Christian’ and Greco-Roman literature used humor as a shared and effective rhetorical technique against their opponents. Writers like Tatian, Celsus, Origen, and Tertullian organized their rhetoric around paideia, polemical tropes, and genre rather than religious affiliation. Her further interests include religious entrepreneurship, Roman law and literature, and the so-called Second Sophistic. Her doctoral research is supported by a Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC) Doctoral Fellowship.

name: Carson Riggs

name: Ariana Rivera
